failing_part: "screening predictors by their univariate association with the outcome may be done once on all rows before cross-validation without biasing the error estimate"
narrowest_regime: None for the supervised screen. The other half needs softening too: outcome-free steps (scaling, PCA, median imputation) are safest fit inside each fold, but HTF 7.10.2 says unsupervised screening done before CV is allowed, so 'must' is stricter than the literature.
reason: A screen on the outcome is a supervised step. Run on all rows, it has already seen each validation fold's outcomes, so CV scores the chosen features on data that helped pick them. That is the selection bias Ambroise & McLachlan 2002 showed with near-zero CV error on noise genes, and HTF 7.10.2's 'wrong way' to cross-validate. 'Only each predictor's marginal association' gives no protection: the marginal association with Y is exactly the leak. The claim's own cited sources say the opposite of what it says.

citations.cite: Ambroise C, McLachlan GJ. Selection bias in gene extraction on the basis of microarray gene-expression data. PNAS 2002;99:6562-6566
Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, Elements of Statistical Learning 2nd ed. 2009, s.7.10.2 'The Wrong and Right Way to Do Cross-validation'

bite_note: Decides whether the screen runs inside each fold or once up front. Up front, CV error with many candidate predictors can be badly optimistic, near zero for pure noise, so the reported performance and the model chosen are wrong.

failing_part: "the primary analysis is per protocol ... because excluding non-adherers removes noise while the comparison stays protected by randomization"
narrowest_regime: None as a primary-analysis rule for superiority trials. Per-protocol is a common secondary or sensitivity analysis, and in non-inferiority trials it is often reported next to ITT, but it never keeps the protection of randomization.
reason: Adherence happens after randomization and is often tied to prognosis. Dropping non-adherers compares groups that are no longer exchangeable, so randomization stops protecting the comparison. CONSORT 2010 E&E says ITT 'is generally favoured because it avoids bias associated with non-random loss of participants' and that per-protocol analyses 'are often considerably flawed'. Item 16, the item cited, only asks authors to report the denominators and whether analysis was by originally assigned groups; it does not endorse per-protocol.

citations.cite: Moher D et al. CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration. BMJ 2010;340:c869 (item 16)

bite_note: Sets the primary analysis population. Per-protocol can reverse or inflate the effect (CONSORT's carotid-surgery example), so the headline estimate changes.

failing_part: "which also serves as a valid prediction interval for a new cycle's MSE when cycles' performance is heterogeneous"
narrowest_regime: A fixed-effect pooled MSE with its normal CI only describes the precision of a common or average MSE when cycles are homogeneous (tau^2 near 0). It is never a prediction interval for a new cycle once there is heterogeneity.
reason: A fixed-effect CI covers only within-cycle sampling error, and its width goes to zero as cycles grow. The spread of a new cycle's true MSE includes the between-cycle variance tau^2, which this interval leaves out. Riley et al. 2016, the source cited, recommends random-effects meta-analysis with a 95% prediction interval to show heterogeneity in performance. Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter 2009 give that interval as mu_hat +/- t_{k-2} sqrt(tau^2_hat + SE(mu_hat)^2). Under heterogeneity, the fixed-effect interval will undercover a new cycle's MSE, often by a lot.

citations.cite: Riley RD et al. External validation of clinical prediction models using big datasets from e-health records or IPD meta-analysis. BMJ 2016;353:i3140
Higgins JPT, Thompson SG, Spiegelhalter DJ. A re-evaluation of random-effects meta-analysis. JRSS-A 2009;172:137-159

bite_note: Researchers would read a narrow interval as the range a new survey cycle's error should fall in, and would wrongly conclude transportability or stable performance.

failing_part: "in one of its groups every row has the event" (not a cause of monotone likelihood in Cox); "beyond 20 SDs ... (or does not converge)" taken as proof of no finite maximum; "no interval or p-value is reported" presented as forced
narrowest_regime: Holds when the likelihood really is monotone: every failure has the extreme covariate value in its risk set, e.g. a binary group with no events, or with all its events after the other group has left the risk set. In that case Wald inference is meaningless and refusing it is right.
reason: Simulation: (a) a group where all 15 rows have the event, with the other group's events interleaved, gives a finite interior maximum (beta*SD about 0.96). The 'every row has the event' half is the logistic-separation condition, not Cox's. (b) A near-monotone continuous covariate gives a finite MLE (score about 0) at beta*SD about 120, so >20 SD is a heuristic, not proof. A Newton fit with coxph-style log-likelihood convergence 'converged' at beta*SD about 11 on truly monotone data, so the trigger can also miss. Under monotone likelihood, Heinze & Schemper 2001 show finite Firth-penalized estimates with penalized-LR tests and profile CIs, and the ordinary LR statistic stays finite, so 'no interval or p-value' is a choice, not a consequence.

citations.cite: Heinze G, Schemper M. A solution to the problem of monotone likelihood in Cox regression. Biometrics 2001;57:114-119
Bryson MC, Johnson ME. The incidence of monotone likelihood in the Cox model. Technometrics 1981;23:381-383

bite_note: The researcher is told the HR is infinite and gets no p-value or CI, where a Firth-penalized HR with a profile-likelihood CI and an LR test would give usable, valid inference. The parenthetical also misdiagnoses the cause, e.g. points to an all-events group.

narrowest_regime: Pairs per person with the true value allowed to change (one-way random-effects model for the differences), unbalanced m_i allowed, no survey design.
reason: Under d_ij = mu + b_i + e_ij, the SD of one difference is sqrt(sigma_b^2 + sigma_w^2). The one-way ANOVA moment estimator uses the unbalanced coefficient n0 = (n^2 - sum m_i^2)/((k-1)n), as in Bland & Altman 1999/2007. The grand mean's variance is exactly (sigma_b^2 sum m_i^2 + sigma_w^2 n)/n^2, by derivation. Zou 2013 gives MOVER CIs for the limits with multiple observations per person. t(k-1) and the person-means fallback after truncation are conservative choices of the app's own: in simulation (k = 8 or 20, m_i from 2 to 7, sigma_b/sigma_w from 0 to 1, truncation in up to 56% of runs) the bias CI covered 0.948-0.956.

citations.cite: Bland JM, Altman DG. Agreement between methods of measurement with multiple observations per individual. J Biopharm Stat 2007;17:571-582
Zou GY. Confidence interval estimation for the Bland-Altman limits of agreement with multiple observations per individual. Stat Methods Med Res 2013;22:630-642
Bland JM, Altman DG. Measuring agreement in method comparison studies. Stat Methods Med Res 1999;8:135-160 (s.5.2, unbalanced ANOVA divisor)

bite_note: Treating repeated pairs as independent understates the SD of a difference when sigma_b > 0. Limits come out too narrow and the bias CI overconfident, which changes whether two methods are judged interchangeable.

failing_part: "views that use the outcome may only add candidates to a declared search under prediction (never prune it)": adding outcome-chosen candidates leaks as much as pruning
narrowest_regime: The outcome-free half and the inference half hold. Outcome-masked data reduction and representation choices are allowed (Harrell's data reduction blind to Y). Outcome-informed findings under inference should be reported, not acted on, unless a selection-aware method (post-double-selection, sample splitting) carries them. Under prediction, outcome views are safe only if they are recomputed inside each training fold, or if the final score comes from rows the views never saw. That protection does not depend on adding vs pruning.
reason: Adding a candidate because an outcome view on all rows liked it is selection on the outcome, the Ambroise-McLachlan leak. Adding the top-1 of 2000 is the same act as pruning the other 1999. Simulation: pure-noise outcome, n = 60, 2000 noise features, a declared search over 5 features, then the top full-data correlate added and the whole search run inside 10-fold CV (150 reps). CV MSE was 0.87 against a true MSE of 1.23 (null 1.0), so CV reported skill that is not there. Without the added candidate, CV was 1.08 against 1.06. The add/prune asymmetry has no methods basis. Separately, if 'imputation rules' means imputation models without the outcome, those attenuate under inference (Moons et al. 2006).

citations.cite: Ambroise C, McLachlan GJ. PNAS 2002;99:6562-6566
Baillie M et al. Ten simple rules for initial data analysis. PLoS Comput Biol 2022;18:e1009819
Belloni A, Chernozhukov V, Hansen C. Inference on treatment effects after selection among high-dimensional controls. Rev Econ Stud 2014;81:608-650
Harrell FE. Regression Modeling Strategies, 2nd ed. 2015, s.4.7 (data reduction)
Gelman A, Loken E. The garden of forking paths, 2013 (tech. report)
Moons KGM et al. Using the outcome for imputation of missing predictor values was preferred. J Clin Epidemiol 2006;59:1092-1101

bite_note: The rule lets an outcome-informed candidate into the search, and its CV score looks good. A researcher can then choose that candidate and report optimistic internal validation; the simulation shows skill reported where none exists.

failing_part: "here 3,916 rows needed for 73 terms at an expected shrinkage of at least 0.9": the figure holds only at an unstated anticipated R^2 of 0.15
narrowest_regime: Continuous outcome, linear-family model, anticipated adjusted R^2 = 0.15. There Riley Part I criterion (i) gives exactly n = 3,916 for p = 73, S >= 0.9, and the other three criteria (1,242; about 307; intercept) do not bind. Harrell-quantile RCS with knots placed per training fold is sound.
reason: Running pmsampsize's continuous-outcome shrinkage formula reproduces 3,916 exactly at R^2_adj = 0.15. The required n moves a lot with R^2: about 6,042 at 0.10, 2,851 at 0.20, 1,782 at 0.30. Riley et al. 2019 say the criteria 'require prespecification of ... the model's anticipated R^2 as informed by previous studies'. The claim states neither the 0.15 nor where it came from; Riley's 0.15 fallback is a Nagelkerke R^2 for binary outcomes, not continuous ones. Spline-by-default under a Riley gate is a defensible convention (Harrell), conservative for ridge and the elastic net, but the gate's precision rests on an unsourced input.

citations.cite: Riley RD et al. Minimum sample size for developing a multivariable prediction model: Part I - continuous outcomes. Stat Med 2019;38:1262-1275
Riley RD et al. Part II - binary and time-to-event outcomes. Stat Med 2019;38:1276-1296
Riley RD et al. Calculating the sample size required for developing a clinical prediction model. BMJ 2020;368:m441
pmsampsize R package, pmsampsize_cont.R (CRAN mirror), criterion (i) formula
Harrell FE. Regression Modeling Strategies, 2nd ed. 2015 (RCS default knot quantiles)

bite_note: The gate decides between curves and straight lines for every continuous predictor. Between about 1,800 and 6,000 rows the decision flips with the assumed R^2, which the researcher never sees.

failing_part: "estimates population performance only if the folds keep whole PSUs within strata and every loss ... is survey-weighted"; also "performance on these rows only"
narrowest_regime: Informative designs, where selection probability relates to the outcome or to prediction error, plus non-trivial within-PSU dependence. There, design-based CV (whole-PSU folds, stratum-balanced, weighted test loss) is the recommended way to estimate population performance.
reason: WGM 2022 claim only that 'we will tend to make better inferences when we choose the folds and compute the test errors in ways that account for the survey design'. That makes design-based CV sufficient and preferred, not necessary. If sampling is non-informative (weights unrelated to (X, Y) and error) and residual clustering is negligible, unweighted row-level CV is consistent for population error. Stratum balance in fold assignment mainly reduces variance; it is not needed for consistency. Under the sample answer, CV estimates expected error on new draws like these rows, not on 'these rows only'.

citations.cite: Wieczorek J, Guerin C, McMahon T. K-fold cross-validation for complex sample surveys. Stat 2022;11:e454
Pfeffermann D. The role of sampling weights when modeling survey data. Int Stat Rev 1993;61:317-337

bite_note: Under informative weights or clustering, the default changes the reported population error and the model ranking. Under non-informative, unclustered designs it mostly costs variance, so the 'only if' framing overstates how much bites.

failing_part: "(its column, ranges set by it ...) selects on the value being explained and biases the estimates" as a blanket rule
narrowest_regime: Rules that drop real outcome values: trimming outcome 'outliers', truncating at clinical ranges, or screens (e.g. Goldberg EI:BMR) whose inputs include the outcome. These truncate or select on Y, or on Y and X together, and bias means, slopes and risk differences. Refusing them in sensitivity analyses, as in the primary, is sound there.
reason: Selection on Y biases most estimands. Simulation: true slope 0.5, trimming |y| < 2 SD gave 0.405 (Hausman & Wise 1977; Hernan et al. 2004). But a plausibility range that removes recording errors arising independently of the true value does not select on the value being explained: dropping 2% gross error codes recovered 0.500, while keeping them gave 0.712. Odds ratios are also invariant to selection that depends on Y alone (Prentice & Pyke 1979). So 'biases the estimates' is not universal, and the refusal also blocks legitimate error cleaning on the outcome.

citations.cite: Hausman JA, Wise DA. Social experimentation, truncated distributions, and efficient estimation. Econometrica 1977;45:919-938
Hernan MA, Hernandez-Diaz S, Robins JM. A structural approach to selection bias. Epidemiology 2004;15:615-625
Prentice RL, Pyke R. Logistic disease incidence models and case-control studies. Biometrika 1979;66:403-411

bite_note: Outcome trimming and outcome screens are refused, which prevents biased sensitivity estimates. The same refusal blocks a plausibility-range cleaning rule on the outcome, so recording errors stay in, unless the app has another missing-code path.

failing_part: "is a safe default under every goal"
narrowest_regime: Tables that really are cohort or cross-sectional observational data, or randomized data. For randomized data the observational lane is conservative: no causal shortcut, and baseline adjustment is harmless. Among the possible defaults it is the least-assumption one for causal language.
reason: If the table was sampled by the outcome (case-control), cohort-style Describe and Predict outputs are biased. Prevalences, absolute risks and the logistic intercept reflect the case:control ratio, not the population (Prentice & Pyke 1979), so a prediction model's calibration is wrong. If the table is matched, an unmatched analysis biases the odds ratio, usually toward the null. Stating the default and listing it for confirmation helps only if the researcher catches it; the estimates are not safe in those designs. The cited basis is internal assertion only.

citations.cite: Prentice RL, Pyke R. Biometrika 1979;66:403-411
Breslow NE, Day NE. Statistical Methods in Cancer Research Vol. I: The analysis of case-control studies. IARC 1980 (matched designs)

bite_note: Matters when the true design is outcome-dependent or matched. There it changes which lane runs, gives wrong absolute risks and calibration under Predict and Describe, and biases odds ratios under matching. For true observational or RCT tables it bites little.

failing_part: "exactly one exposure-role column" equated with a family of one hypothesis
narrowest_regime: One exposure column that yields one test (a binary or linearly coded continuous exposure, or a single joint test per column) and one outcome. Then Bonferroni, Holm, Hochberg, BH and Sidak all return the raw p-value and an unadjusted CI.
reason: With one hypothesis, every FWER or FDR procedure reduces to the identity, which is a derivation. But one column can carry several tested parameters: a k-level categorical exposure (k-1 contrasts), spline or polynomial terms, or several outcomes or time points. Over k-1 >= 2 contrasts, Bonferroni, Holm and none give different p-values and intervals. Column count is only a proxy for family size, and the claim offers no basis beyond the family's definition.
bite_note: Where the claim holds (single-df exposure), moving the default to For the record changes no number. It would bite only for multi-df exposures, where a consequential choice would skip confirmation.

narrowest_regime: Columns in the ambiguous zone: many-label strings that repeat across rows (a 70-label category vs a code or free text), positive numeric columns (weight vs measurement), and integer group codes (PSU or stratum vs a categorical predictor).
reason: A role is design metadata, not a property of the value distribution. A sampling weight and a positive measurement such as income can share any distribution, and a PSU code and a categorical predictor are both repeated integer labels. A 70-label country variable has the label count of a short identifier. Value heuristics can raise or lower suspicion (near-unique strings suggest text; weights may sum to a population total), but they cannot decide the role. Getting it wrong has real costs, so asking the user to confirm is the methodologically correct response.
bite_note: Guessing would either drop a real predictor or confounder (country of birth) or put a survey weight or PSU code in as a predictor and leave it out of the design. Either changes the model and its inference.

narrowest_regime: Workflows where estimates first become visible at the plan lock (Estimate, Describe), or held-out scores first become visible when the seal opens (Predict). The gates must coincide with first exposure to the numbers that matter.
reason: A decision made after the target estimates or held-out scores are visible can depend on them: the forking-paths problem. Pre-specification guidance therefore separates pre-specified from post hoc choices instead of letting post hoc choices pass as planned. Refusing a bulk 'Confirm all' after the gate, and recording each noticing individually as made after the numbers were seen, follows from that. Putting the Predict gate at the seal rather than at CV is consistent: decisions informed by CV still leave the held-out estimate unbiased. The basis given is internal only, but the reasoning holds as a derivation.

citations.cite: Gelman A, Loken E. The garden of forking paths, 2013 (tech. report)
ICH E9 Statistical principles for clinical trials, 1998 (pre-specification vs post hoc analyses)

bite_note: Late dispositions get labelled post hoc in the record instead of passing as planned, which changes how a reader weighs those analysis choices. The estimates themselves do not change.
